sections.h2: Launch Hoodies on a Virtual Model
paras: A Tuesday launch of six hoodies can go up while the last hem is still being sewn. You do not need a person in the room to wear them that morning.
A photo of the hoodie on the table is the source. You choose an adult and a room, and the hoodie appears on that person. The image can help a shopper see the collar and the zipper.
sections.alt: Adult woman with short copper hair wearing a plain gray hoodie on an autumn city sidewalk.

paras: Once a flat photo exists, the hoodie can go on an adult without a studio booking. Lay the piece flat, or hang it on a bare wall, shoot it from the front in daylight, and steam the wrinkles you can see.

Creases in that photo can turn into odd folds on the person. Get the whole garment in the frame, including the sleeves, the hem, and the collar. Turn a print toward the camera. Photograph buttons and the zipper side so they are easy to count later. If the first shot is soft, retake it before you open the [photo tools](page:photo-hub).
sections.alt: Hands smooth a plain gray hoodie beside a wooden hanger on a light surface.

sections.h2: One Virtual Model Face on Every Channel
paras: The next piece keeps the same face, so the set looks like one shoot. Name that person once, the way you would name a regular model for the shop.

Put that saved person on the [marketplace listing](page:plat-amazon) and on an [Instagram post](page:plat-instagram), not only on your product page. A ring or glasses can share that face. Write a short pose line, such as hair back and the zipper easy to see. Then check the collar against the hoodie on your table.

sections.h2: Use the Same Path for Jewelry
paras: Use a close, sharp photo of the piece on a plain surface. Keep the clasp, the stones, and the chain easy to see. Save the look if the next piece should be on the same person.

A short line is enough. Try a close side view, hair back, soft window light, and the earring easy to see. In the result, count the stones and check the clasp. See whether a necklace sits where it should, and whether the chain length still matches the piece you photographed.

A shopper can see that the gray hoodie falls at the hip and that the sleeve ends where it should. That is a picture, not a promise that a size medium will fit them. Keep the size chart on the listing.

Compare each image with the real hoodie before it goes on the site. Check the neckline, the sleeve and hem length, where any print sits, the number of pockets, and which side the zipper is on. Stripes and plaids should not bend in a way the cloth cannot. The hood should sit where it sits on the real piece. If a cuff changed shape, run that color again from a sharper photo. The picture can help a shopper see the drape. It does not replace your measurements or the size line on the listing. After the hem check, the same file can also feed [ad images](page:social-ad-photos).

sections.h2: Make the Whole Color Set Together
paras: When one hoodie arrives in more than one color, run them together with the same saved look and the same scene. Review every file before it goes on the site.

Pair the worn photos with a flat photo from the [photo tools](page:photo-hub). Add a room scene from [lifestyle photos](page:lifestyle-photos). Add a plain backdrop from the [background tool](page:change-background). A second color can start from the [color variant](page:tpl-color) once the first hoodie looks right. [Fashion listings](page:ind-fashion-clothing) can use the same set. Review each file. A generated color may not match the swatch in your hand, so compare before you post.

sections.h2: How to Make Model Photos in 3 Simple Steps
paras: Upload your product photo. Steam the hoodie and photograph it so the collar and both sleeves are in the frame. A hanger against a bare wall works. A photo of someone already wearing it works too.
Describe your scene. Decide the room before the pose. A kitchen stool reads differently from a white wall. The hoodie still comes from your photo, and you can save that person for the next color.
Download and post. Square fits the gallery. Choose a tall or wide frame when the channel asks for it. Then check the neckline, length, print, and zippers against the real piece.

faq.q: How does a flat hoodie photo become an on-model picture?
faq.a: Photograph the garment so the whole piece is in frame, choose the adult you saved, and name the room. Then compare the collar, hem, and zipper with the real piece before you post.

faq.q: Can I put the clothing I sell on a generated adult?
faq.a: Yes. The garment in the picture is yours. You choose who wears it, and you can save that person for the next color in the set.

faq.q: Can one saved face stay through my whole lookbook?
faq.a: Only when you pick the saved person again. A new description can grow a different face. Keep a note of the name you saved so the next piece starts there.

faq.q: How close is an on-model photo to a studio shoot?
faq.a: It puts the garment on a person in a room you name. It can look like a catalog photo. Check the neckline, length, print, and zippers. It does not replace a fit model or your size chart.

faq.q: Can my shop software send these photos through the API?
faq.a: Yes. A catalog can send products through the API and get the on-model photos back. Your own system can start that work for the next color.

faq.q: Do I need to say the person in the photo is generated before I post?
faq.a: Check the current disclosure rule for the site where the image will appear. Rules differ, and they change. When a label is required, add it before you post.

faq.q: What photo should I start from for clothing or jewelry?
faq.a: Use a sharp, front-facing photo with the whole garment visible. Smooth wrinkles and use even light. For jewelry, keep the clasp, stones, and chain easy to see.

faq.q: How many credits does one on-model photo use?
faq.a: One photo uses 24 credits. The cost shows before you start. If the job fails, the credits come back. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits, Pro is $35 for 300, and Premium is $63 for 600.
